intro: A phone plan charges a fee plus a price per gigabyte. A candle burns down a set amount every hour. A bike rider's distance grows with every minute on the trail. In each case one amount depends on another in a steady way, and a straight line on a graph captures the whole relationship. This unit is about those lines: what their steepness means, how to write their equations, and how to read them.

You will start with slope, the single number that says how fast a line rises or falls, and you will see why that number is the same between any two points on a line. Then you will meet functions, rules that give exactly one output for each input, and learn to move between words, tables, equations and graphs. Finally you will put two lines on one grid and find the point they share, which answers questions like when one runner catches another or how much data makes two plans cost the same.

By the end you will be able to write the equation of any line from a graph, a table or two points, tell a linear function from a nonlinear one, compare two functions given in different forms, and solve a system of equations three ways. These are the tools that algebra, science and everyday planning all lean on.
bigQuestion: How can a single line, and the place where two lines meet, describe how quantities change and when they agree?

test.q: What is the slope of the line through (2, 5) and (6, 17)?
For y = −3x + 8, what are the slope and the y-intercept?
test.why: In y = mx + b, m is the coefficient of x, −3, and b is the added number, 8.

test.q: What is the equation of the line through (0, −2) and (3, 7)?
test.why: Slope = (7 − (−2)) ÷ (3 − 0) = 9/3 = 3. The y-intercept is −2 because (0, −2) is on the y-axis.

test.q: Which equation shows a proportional relationship?
test.why: A proportional relationship has the form y = kx and passes through the origin. Only y = 2x has no added number.

test.q: What is the equation of the horizontal line through (4, −1)?
test.why: On a horizontal line every point has the same y-value. Here that value is −1, so the equation is y = −1.

test.q: Which list of pairs is NOT a function?
test.why: The input 2 has two outputs, 1 and 3. One input with two outputs breaks the rule for a function.

test.q: A table shows x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 1, 4, 9. Which describes the function?
choices: nonlinear, because the changes 3 and 5 are not equal
test.why: 4 − 1 = 3 and 9 − 4 = 5. The changes differ, so the rate is not constant and the function is nonlinear (it is y = x^2).

test.q: A linear function has x = 1, y = 14 and x = 3, y = 22. What is its initial value?
test.why: Rate = (22 − 14) ÷ (3 − 1) = 4. Going back one step from x = 1: 14 − 4 = 10. So y = 4x + 10 and the initial value is 10.

test.q: On a graph of distance from home against time, what does a flat segment mean?
choices: the person moved at a steady speed
the fastest part of the trip
test.why: A flat segment has slope 0, so the distance is not changing. The person is not moving.

test.q: Function A is y = 6x + 1. Function B is the table x = 0, 1, 2 and y = 4, 9, 14. Which has the greater rate of change?
test.why: B's rate is 9 − 4 = 5 per step. A's rate is 6. So A changes faster.

test.q: Solve the system y = x + 4 and y = 3x.
test.why: 3x = x + 4 gives 2x = 4, so x = 2 and y = 3 × 2 = 6. Check: 2 + 4 = 6.

test.q: Solve x + y = 11 and x − y = 3.
test.why: Adding gives 2x = 14, so x = 7. Then y = 11 − 7 = 4. Check: 7 − 4 = 3.

test.q: How many solutions does y = 5x − 2 and y = 5x + 6 have?
test.why: Both lines have slope 5 with different y-intercepts, so they are parallel and never meet.

test.q: Solve y = 2x and x + y = 18 by substitution.
test.why: x + 2x = 18 gives 3x = 18, so x = 6 and y = 2 × 6 = 12. Check: 6 + 12 = 18.

test.q: Plan A costs $30 plus $3 per GB. Plan B costs $15 plus $6 per GB. When do they cost the same?

write.prompt: Two gyms: Gym A charges $40 to join and $15 a month. Gym B charges no joining fee and $25 a month. Write an equation for each gym, find the number of months when the two cost the same, and explain which gym is cheaper for someone who plans to stay one year. Show every step.

title: Functions and Linear Equations

chapters.title: Linear Equations and Slope
chapters.bigQuestion: How can one number describe how steep a line is, and how does that number show up in the line's equation?

story.title: Two Hills, Two Staircases
story.kicker: Two sets of stairs climb the same height, but one leaves you out of breath. A single number explains why.
paragraphs: Maya's school in Chicago has two staircases that go from the first floor to the second. Both climb the same 12 feet. The front stairs are long and gentle. The back stairs, near the gym, are short and steep. Every student knows which one to take when carrying a heavy backpack. Nobody had ever measured why the back stairs feel so much harder.

In math class, Maya's teacher asked the class to measure both. The front stairs rise 12 feet while stretching 20 feet along the floor. The back stairs rise the same 12 feet but stretch only 10 feet along the floor. The class wrote the two measurements as fractions: 12/20 for the front and 12/10 for the back. Written as decimals, that is 0.6 and 1.2. The back stairs climb twice as much for every foot forward.

That fraction, the rise divided by the run, is called the slope. Road signs use the same idea. A sign that says 8% grade means the road rises 8 feet for every 100 feet you drive forward. A bike path along Lake Michigan is nearly flat, so its slope is close to 0. A ramp for wheelchairs is built so that it rises no more than 1 foot for every 12 feet of length, a slope of 1/12.

Maya noticed something else. The front staircase has 16 steps, and each step is the same size. She measured one step: it rises 9 inches and runs 15 inches. That is 9/15, which equals 0.6, the same slope as the whole staircase. It did not matter whether she measured one step or all sixteen. On a straight line, the slope is the same everywhere. That fact is the key to this whole chapter.

By the end of the chapter, you will be able to look at any straight line on a graph and name its slope. You will write its equation, predict where it goes, and tell a steep climb from a gentle one with a single number. The two staircases are only the start.
story.think: The front stairs rise 12 feet over 20 feet of floor, and the back stairs rise 12 feet over 10 feet. If a third staircase rose 12 feet over 15 feet, where would it fit between them, and how do you know?

lessons.title: Rise Over Run
lessons.mainIdea: Slope is the rise divided by the run, and a bigger slope means a steeper climb.
reading: Picture one step of a staircase. The step goes up a certain height and forward a certain distance. The height it goes up is the *rise*. The distance it goes forward is the *run*. The *slope* is the rise divided by the run. A step that rises 7 inches and runs 11 inches has a slope of 7/11. If you write that as a decimal, 7 ÷ 11 is about 0.64.

Try a wheelchair ramp. A ramp rises 2 feet from the sidewalk to a door, and it stretches 24 feet along the ground. Slope = rise ÷ run = 2/24. Simplify by dividing the top and bottom by 2: 2/24 = 1/12. That is the gentlest slope most building rules allow for a ramp, so this ramp passes. A ramp that rose 2 feet over only 12 feet would have slope 2/12 = 1/6, twice as steep, and it would be hard to push a chair up.

Slope lets you compare steepness even when the numbers look different. Hill A rises 30 feet over 200 feet: 30/200 = 0.15. Hill B rises 12 feet over 60 feet: 12/60 = 0.2. Hill B is steeper, even though it rises fewer feet, because it does its rising in a shorter distance. To compare slopes, turn each fraction into a decimal or give them the same denominator.

The most common mistake is flipping the fraction and putting run over rise. A ramp with rise 2 and run 24 has slope 2/24, not 24/2 = 12. Remember that a gentle ramp should have a small slope number. If your answer for a gentle ramp is a big number, you flipped it. A second mistake is mixing units, like rise in inches and run in feet. Change both to the same unit before you divide.

words.d: the rise divided by the run; a number that tells how steep a line or ramp is
how far something goes up (or down) between two points
how far something goes forward, or sideways, between two points

look.title: Planning a Ramp
look.text: A library needs a ramp to a side door that is 30 inches above the sidewalk. The rule is that the slope may be no more than 1/12. The builder wants to know the shortest run that works. Set up the fraction: 30 ÷ run = 1/12. The run must be 12 times the rise, so run = 30 × 12 = 360 inches, which is 30 feet. A run shorter than 360 inches would make the slope larger than 1/12.
look.prompt: If the door were 24 inches above the sidewalk instead, what is the shortest run that keeps the slope at 1/12 or less? Give your answer in inches and in feet.

check.q: A ramp rises 3 feet over a run of 36 feet. What is its slope?
check.why: Slope = rise ÷ run = 3/36. Divide top and bottom by 3 to get 1/12. The answer 12 comes from flipping the fraction.

check.q: Staircase A rises 6 feet over a run of 8 feet. Staircase B rises 6 feet over a run of 12 feet. Which is steeper, and why?
choices: B, because its run is longer
They are the same, because both rise 6 feet
check.why: Compare the slopes: 6/8 = 0.75 and 6/12 = 0.5. The larger slope, 0.75, belongs to A, so A is steeper.

check.q: One step rises 7 inches and runs 10 inches. What is the slope as a decimal?
check.why: Slope = 7 ÷ 10 = 0.7. The answer 1.43 comes from 10 ÷ 7, and 17 comes from adding instead of dividing.

lessons.title: Slope Between Two Points
lessons.mainIdea: To find the slope between two points, subtract the y-values for the rise and the x-values for the run, in the same order.
reading: On a graph, every point is an *ordered pair* (x, y). The x tells how far right, and the y tells how far up. To find the slope of the line through two points, find the rise by subtracting the y-values and the run by subtracting the x-values. Take the points (2, 3) and (6, 11). Rise = 11 − 3 = 8. Run = 6 − 2 = 4. Slope = 8/4 = 2. The line goes up 2 for every 1 it goes right.

The order matters, but only in one way: subtract in the same order on top and bottom. With (2, 3) and (6, 11), you could also do rise = 3 − 11 = −8 and run = 2 − 6 = −4. Then slope = −8/−4 = 2. Same answer. The mistake is mixing the orders, like 11 − 3 on top and 2 − 6 on the bottom, which gives 8/−4 = −2 and the wrong sign.

Lines can go downhill too. Take (1, 9) and (4, 3). Rise = 3 − 9 = −6. Run = 4 − 1 = 3. Slope = −6/3 = −2. A *negative slope* means the line drops as you move right: down 2 for every 1 to the right. On a graph of a car's gas tank over time, the slope is negative because the gas goes down as time goes up.

Here is the rule in general. For points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2), slope = (y2 − y1) ÷ (x2 − x1). Say it as change in y over change in x. One more check: the run is always the x part. A student who writes (x2 − x1) on top has flipped the fraction and will get the wrong slope.

words.d: two numbers in order, (x, y), that name a point on a graph
a slope less than 0; the line goes down as you move to the right

look.title: Points on One Line
look.cite: Table of values from the line y = 3x + 1, made for this lesson
look.prompt: Pick any two rows and find the slope between them. Then pick two different rows and do it again. What do you notice about the two answers?

check.q: What is the slope of the line through (1, 2) and (5, 10)?
check.why: Rise = 10 − 2 = 8. Run = 5 − 1 = 4. Slope = 8/4 = 2. The answer 1/2 comes from putting run over rise.

check.q: What is the slope of the line through (2, 7) and (6, 3)?
check.why: Rise = 3 − 7 = −4. Run = 6 − 2 = 4. Slope = −4/4 = −1. Dropping the sign gives the wrong answer 1.

check.q: A student finds the slope between (1, 4) and (3, 10) as (3 − 1) ÷ (10 − 4) = 1/3. What mistake did the student make?
choices: Put the run over the rise instead of the rise over the run
check.why: The student divided the change in x by the change in y. The correct slope is (10 − 4) ÷ (3 − 1) = 6/2 = 3.

lessons.title: Same Slope Everywhere
lessons.mainIdea: Every slope triangle on a straight line is similar to every other one, so the slope is the same between any two points.
reading: Draw a line through (0, 0), (2, 3), (4, 6) and (6, 9). Now draw a right triangle under the line from (0, 0) to (2, 3): its legs are the run 2 and the rise 3. This is a *slope triangle*. Draw a bigger one from (0, 0) to (6, 9): run 6 and rise 9. The big triangle is just the small one enlarged by 3. Its slope is 9/6, and 9/6 simplifies to 3/2, the same as the small triangle's 3/2.

Triangles that are enlargements of each other are *similar triangles*. They have the same angles, and their matching sides are in the same ratio. Every slope triangle on one line has the same angle at the bottom, because the line always tilts the same way. So all the slope triangles are similar, and rise ÷ run comes out the same for every one of them. This is why a straight line has exactly one slope.

You can use this fact to test whether points are on one line. Take (1, 1), (3, 5) and (6, 11). From the first to the second: rise 4, run 2, slope 2. From the second to the third: rise 6, run 3, slope 2. Same slope, so the three points sit on one line. Now try (0, 1), (2, 5) and (5, 10). First pair: 4/2 = 2. Second pair: 5/3. Different slopes, so these three points do not line up.

A common mistake is to think a bigger slope triangle means a bigger slope. The triangle from (0, 0) to (6, 9) is three times as large as the one to (2, 3), but its slope is still 3/2. Slope is a ratio, and a ratio does not change when you scale both parts. Another mistake is checking only the y-values. Points whose y-values grow by the same amount are on a line only if their x-values also grow by the same amount.

words.d: a right triangle drawn between two points on a line, with the run as one leg and the rise as the other
triangles with the same angles whose matching sides are in the same ratio

look.title: Are They on One Line?
look.text: Three points are plotted: (1, 1), (3, 5) and (6, 11). Between the first two, the slope triangle has run 2 and rise 4, so the slope is 4/2 = 2. Between the last two, the run is 3 and the rise is 6, so the slope is 6/3 = 2. The two slopes match, so the three points are on one straight line.
look.prompt: A fourth point is (10, 19). Find the slope from (6, 11) to (10, 19). Is the fourth point on the same line? Explain using the slope.

check.q: A slope triangle from (0, 0) to (4, 2) has rise 2 and run 4. A larger slope triangle on the same line has run 12. What is its rise?
check.why: The slope is 2/4 = 1/2. With run 12, rise = 12 × 1/2 = 6. The triangles are similar, so the ratio stays 1/2.

check.q: Why does a straight line have the same slope between any two of its points?
choices: Because every line goes through the origin
Because the rise is always positive
Because all the slope triangles are the same size
Because all the slope triangles on a line are similar, so rise ÷ run is the same for each
check.why: Similar triangles have sides in the same ratio. Rise ÷ run is that ratio, so it is equal for every slope triangle on the line.

check.q: Are the points (0, 1), (2, 5) and (5, 10) on one straight line?
choices: No, the slopes 2 and 5/3 are different
Yes, because all the y-values grow
Yes, because the slope is 2 everywhere
No, because 5 is an odd number
check.why: From (0, 1) to (2, 5): 4/2 = 2. From (2, 5) to (5, 10): 5/3. Different slopes mean the points are not on one line.

lessons.title: Slope as a Rate of Change
lessons.mainIdea: In a real situation, the slope is the rate of change: how much y changes for each 1 unit of x.
reading: Dev works at a car wash. After 2 hours he has earned $30. After 5 hours he has earned $75. How much does he earn *per* hour? The pay went up 75 − 30 = 45 dollars while the time went up 5 − 2 = 3 hours. So the *rate of change* is 45 ÷ 3 = 15 dollars per hour. That is exactly the slope between the points (2, 30) and (5, 75): rise 45, run 3, slope 15.

The rate of change always carries units. Here it is dollars per hour. Try a water tank. After 3 minutes it holds 40 gallons. After 8 minutes it holds 90 gallons. Change in gallons: 90 − 40 = 50. Change in minutes: 8 − 3 = 5. Rate = 50 ÷ 5 = 10 gallons per minute. On a graph with minutes on the x-axis and gallons on the y-axis, the slope of the line is 10.

Notice what the rate does not tell you. It does not say how much water was in the tank at the start. Work backward: at 3 minutes there were 40 gallons, and the tank gains 10 per minute, so at 0 minutes there were 40 − 30 = 10 gallons. The rate tells the speed of change, and the starting amount is a separate fact. You will need both to write the equation of a line in the next lesson.

Watch for the mistake of dividing the wrong way. A student who computes 3 ÷ 45 for Dev's pay gets 0.067 hours per dollar, which is a real number but not the question asked. Always divide the change in the output (pay, gallons) by the change in the input (hours, minutes). Another mistake is dividing the totals, like 75 ÷ 5 = 15. That happens to work here only because Dev started at $0. It fails for the tank: 90 ÷ 8 is 11.25, not 10.

words.d: how much the output changes for each 1 unit of input; on a graph, the slope
for each one; 60 miles per hour means 60 miles for each 1 hour

look.title: A Data Plan
look.cite: Example phone plan made for this lesson: $20 a month plus $5 for each gigabyte of data
look.prompt: What is the rate of change in dollars per gigabyte? What does the $20 in the first row mean? How much would 10 GB cost?

check.q: A car has gone 120 miles after 2 hours and 300 miles after 5 hours. What is its rate of change in miles per hour?
check.why: Change in miles: 300 − 120 = 180. Change in hours: 5 − 2 = 3. Rate = 180 ÷ 3 = 60 miles per hour.

check.q: A tank holds 40 gallons at 3 minutes and 90 gallons at 8 minutes. What is the rate of change?
check.why: (90 − 40) ÷ (8 − 3) = 50 ÷ 5 = 10 gallons per minute. Dividing 90 by 8 gives 11.25, which ignores the water already there.

check.q: On a graph with time on the x-axis and distance on the y-axis, what does the slope of the line tell you?
check.why: Slope is change in distance divided by change in time, and distance per time is speed.

lessons.title: The Form y = mx + b
lessons.mainIdea: In y = mx + b, m is the slope and b is the y-intercept, the value of y when x is 0.
reading: A taxi charges $3 just to get in, then $2 for every mile. The cost y for x miles is y = 2x + 3. Try 4 miles: y = 2 × 4 + 3 = 8 + 3 = 11 dollars. Try 0 miles: y = 2 × 0 + 3 = 3 dollars, the starting fee. The number multiplied by x, here 2, is the slope: cost goes up $2 for each mile. The number added at the end, here 3, is the *y-intercept*: the value of y when x is 0, where the line crosses the y-axis.

The general form is y = mx + b. It is called *slope-intercept form* because m is the slope and b is the y-intercept. The m is a *coefficient*, a number multiplied by a variable. So y = 5x + 2 has slope 5 and y-intercept 2. A negative slope works the same way: y = −3x + 10 has slope −3 and y-intercept 10. Put in x = 2: y = −3 × 2 + 10 = −6 + 10 = 4.

The order of the terms can trick you. The equation y = 7 + 4x has slope 4, not 7, because 4 is the number attached to x. The 7 is added alone, so it is the y-intercept. Rewrite it as y = 4x + 7 if that helps. Likewise y = x − 6 has slope 1, because x means 1x, and its y-intercept is −6.

A gym charges $25 to join and $10 each month. Write the equation: the rate is 10 per month, and the starting amount is 25, so y = 10x + 25, where x is the number of months. After 6 months: y = 10 × 6 + 25 = 60 + 25 = 85 dollars. The mistake to avoid is swapping m and b: y = 25x + 10 would mean $25 every month, which is a very different gym.

words.d: the value of y when x is 0; the point where a line crosses the y-axis
the equation of a line written as y = mx + b, with slope m and y-intercept b
a number multiplied by a variable, like the 4 in 4x

look.title: The Gym Bill
look.text: A gym charges $25 to join and then $10 every month. Let x be the number of months and y the total paid. The rate is $10 per month, so m = 10. At 0 months you have paid only the $25 fee, so b = 25. The equation is y = 10x + 25. After 6 months, y = 10 × 6 + 25 = 85 dollars.
look.prompt: Use the equation to find the total paid after 12 months. Then explain what changes in the equation if the joining fee goes up to $40 but the monthly price stays the same.

check.q: In the equation y = 5x + 2, what are the slope and the y-intercept?
check.why: In y = mx + b, m is the number multiplied by x (5) and b is the number added (2).

check.q: For y = −2x + 9, what is y when x = 3?
check.why: y = −2 × 3 + 9 = −6 + 9 = 3. Forgetting the negative sign gives 6 + 9 = 15.

check.q: Which equation has slope 3 and y-intercept −4?
check.why: The slope 3 must multiply x, and the y-intercept −4 is added: y = 3x + (−4) = 3x − 4.

lessons.title: Graphing From Slope and Intercept
lessons.mainIdea: To graph y = mx + b, plot the y-intercept, then use the slope as rise over run to find more points.
reading: To *graph* y = (2/3)x + 1, start at the y-intercept. The y-intercept is 1, so *plot* the point (0, 1) on the *y-axis*. Next use the slope 2/3 as directions: rise 2, run 3. From (0, 1), go right 3 and up 2 to reach (3, 3). Do it again to reach (6, 5). Draw a straight line through the points. Check one: at x = 3, y = (2/3) × 3 + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3. Correct.

A whole-number slope is a fraction with 1 on the bottom. For y = 4x − 2, the slope is 4/1: rise 4, run 1. Start at (0, −2), go right 1 and up 4 to (1, 2), then to (2, 6). A negative slope means go down instead of up. For y = −x + 4, the slope is −1, so rise −1, run 1. Start at (0, 4), go right 1 and down 1 to (1, 3), then (2, 2), then (3, 1), and at (4, 0) the line crosses the x-axis.

Now try y = −(1/2)x + 5. Start at (0, 5). The slope −1/2 means right 2, down 1. That gives (2, 4), then (4, 3), (6, 2), (8, 1) and (10, 0). Check with the equation: at x = 10, y = −(1/2) × 10 + 5 = −5 + 5 = 0. So the line hits the x-axis at (10, 0).

Two mistakes come up often. First, starting on the x-axis: the y-intercept 1 is the point (0, 1), not (1, 0). Second, reading the slope upside down: for 2/3, go up 2 and right 3, not up 3 and right 2. If you go the wrong way, the line will be steeper or flatter than it should be. Always test one of your points in the equation before you draw the line.

words.d: to draw a line or points on a coordinate grid so you can see the equation
to mark a point at its (x, y) location on a grid
the vertical number line on a graph, where x is 0

look.title: Down to the x-Axis
look.text: Graph y = −(1/2)x + 5. Start at the y-intercept (0, 5). The slope is −1/2, so each move is right 2 and down 1. The points are (2, 4), (4, 3), (6, 2), (8, 1) and (10, 0). Drawing the line through them shows it crossing the x-axis at (10, 0).
look.prompt: Graph y = −(1/2)x + 5 yourself on grid paper and mark where it crosses the x-axis. Then predict where y = −(1/2)x + 3 crosses the x-axis, and check by graphing.

check.q: To graph y = (3/4)x − 2, which point do you plot first?
check.why: The y-intercept is −2, and it sits on the y-axis where x = 0, so the first point is (0, −2).

check.q: A line starts at (0, 1) with slope 2/5. Which point comes next using rise over run?
check.why: Slope 2/5 means right 5 and up 2. From (0, 1) that is (0 + 5, 1 + 2) = (5, 3). The point (2, 6) comes from reading the slope upside down.

check.q: Which point is on the line y = −3x + 6?
check.why: At x = 1, y = −3 × 1 + 6 = 3, so (1, 3) is on the line. The point (1, 9) comes from forgetting the negative sign.

lessons.title: Equation From a Graph
lessons.mainIdea: Read the y-intercept where the line crosses the y-axis, find the slope from two clear points, then write y = mx + b.
reading: A line is drawn on a grid. To write its equation, find two things: where it crosses the y-axis and how steep it is. Say the line crosses the y-axis at 2 and also passes through (4, 5). The y-intercept is b = 2. For the slope, draw a slope triangle from (0, 2) to (4, 5): rise 5 − 2 = 3, run 4 − 0 = 4, slope 3/4. The equation is y = (3/4)x + 2.

Choose points where the line passes exactly through a grid corner. Such a point is called a *lattice point*, and it gives whole-number coordinates you can trust. A point where the line passes between grid corners is a guess, and a guess makes the slope wrong. Two lattice points far apart give the most accurate slope.

Now a line that falls. It crosses the y-axis at 6 and crosses the x-axis at 3. The place it crosses the x-axis is the *x-intercept*, the point (3, 0). Slope from (0, 6) to (3, 0): rise 0 − 6 = −6, run 3 − 0 = 3, slope −2. Equation: y = −2x + 6. Check with the x-intercept: y = −2 × 3 + 6 = 0. Correct.

The most common error is using the x-intercept as b. In the example above, a student might write y = −2x + 3 because the line hits the x-axis at 3. Test it: at x = 0 that equation gives y = 3, but the line is at 6 when x = 0. The b in y = mx + b is always where the line crosses the y-axis. Always test your equation with a point you can see on the graph.

words.d: a point on a grid where both coordinates are whole numbers
the point where a line crosses the x-axis, where y is 0

look.title: Reading a Line
look.text: Picture a line on grid paper. It crosses the y-axis at −1, so it passes through (0, −1). Farther along, it passes exactly through the grid corner (2, 5). Slope triangle: rise 5 − (−1) = 6, run 2 − 0 = 2, slope 6/2 = 3. So b = −1 and m = 3, and the equation is y = 3x − 1.
look.prompt: Check the equation y = 3x − 1 with the point (4, 11). Then describe what the graph of y = 3x + 1 would look like compared with this line.

check.q: A line passes through (0, 3) and (2, 7). What is its equation?
check.why: b = 3 because the line is at y = 3 when x = 0. Slope = (7 − 3) ÷ (2 − 0) = 4/2 = 2. So y = 2x + 3.

check.q: A line crosses the y-axis at 8 and the x-axis at 4. What is its equation?
check.why: From (0, 8) to (4, 0): rise −8, run 4, slope −2. b is 8, the y-intercept. So y = −2x + 8.

check.q: A student writes the x-intercept as b in y = mx + b. What goes wrong?
choices: The equation gives the wrong y when x = 0
Nothing, the two intercepts are always the same
check.why: b must equal y when x is 0. Using the x-intercept puts the line at the wrong height, so it misses the real y-intercept.

lessons.title: Equation From a Table or Two Points
lessons.mainIdea: Find the slope from any two points, then substitute one point into y = mx + b to solve for b.
reading: A table shows x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 7, 10, 13. Each time x goes up by 1, y goes up by 3, so the slope is 3. But the table does not show x = 0, so you cannot read b directly. Take any row and *substitute* it into y = 3x + b. Using (1, 7): 7 = 3 × 1 + b, so 7 = 3 + b and b = 4. The equation is y = 3x + 4. Check another row: 3 × 3 + 4 = 13. Correct.

Two points work the same way. Take (2, 1) and (6, 9). Slope = (9 − 1) ÷ (6 − 2) = 8/4 = 2. Now *solve for b* using (2, 1): 1 = 2 × 2 + b, so 1 = 4 + b and b = 1 − 4 = −3. The equation is y = 2x − 3. Check with the other point: 2 × 6 − 3 = 12 − 3 = 9. It matches, so the equation is right.

Here is the whole method in three steps. One: find the slope from two points. Two: put the slope and one point into y = mx + b and solve for b. Three: check with the other point. If the check fails, the slope or b is wrong, and it is worth redoing both.

The trap in a table is grabbing the first y-value as b. In the table above, the first row is (1, 7), and 7 is not the y-intercept, because x is 1 there, not 0. The y-intercept is 4. The only time you can read b straight from a table is when a row has x = 0. Otherwise, substitute and solve.

words.d: to replace a variable with a number you know, like putting x = 1 and y = 7 into an equation
to work out the value of b that makes the equation true for a known point

look.title: A Table Without Zero
look.cite: Table of values from a line made for this lesson
look.prompt: Find the slope from two rows. Then use one row to solve for b and write the equation. Why is 11 not the y-intercept?

check.q: A table shows x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 5, 8, 11. What is the equation of the line?
check.why: Slope is 3 because y rises 3 for each 1 in x. Using (1, 5): 5 = 3 × 1 + b gives b = 2. So y = 3x + 2.

check.q: What is the equation of the line through (1, 4) and (3, 10)?
What is the equation of the line through (0, −2) and (5, 13)?
check.why: Slope = (13 − (−2)) ÷ (5 − 0) = 15/5 = 3. The point (0, −2) is on the y-axis, so b = −2. So y = 3x − 2.

lessons.title: Proportional or Just Linear?
lessons.mainIdea: A proportional relationship is a line through the origin, y = kx; a line with a nonzero y-intercept is linear but not proportional.
reading: Two jobs pay $15 an hour. The first pays only that: y = 15x. The second also gives a $20 bonus on day one: y = 15x + 20. Both graphs are lines with slope 15. But only the first goes through the *origin*, the point (0, 0). At 0 hours the first job pays $0 and the second pays $20. The first is a *proportional relationship*; the second is linear but not proportional.

In a proportional relationship, y is always the same multiple of x. The equation is y = kx, and k is the *constant of proportionality*. It is also the slope, and the y-intercept is 0. To test a table, divide each y by its x. Try x = 2, 4, 6 with y = 10, 20, 30: 10/2 = 5, 20/4 = 5, 30/6 = 5. Same every time, so it is proportional with k = 5, and y = 5x.

Now test x = 2, 4 with y = 12, 18. Divide: 12/2 = 6 and 18/4 = 4.5. Not the same, so it is not proportional. Is it still a line? From (2, 12) to (4, 18) the slope is 6/2 = 3. Solve for b: 12 = 3 × 2 + b, so b = 6. The equation is y = 3x + 6. It is a line, but it does not pass through the origin, so it is not proportional.

Students often say a table is proportional because y goes up by the same amount each time. That only shows the relationship is linear. Proportional needs more: y ÷ x must be the same for every row, which is the same as saying the line passes through (0, 0). Every proportional relationship is linear, but most linear relationships are not proportional.

words.d: a relationship where y is always the same multiple of x, so y = kx and the graph passes through (0, 0)
the number k in y = kx; the value of y ÷ x, which is also the slope
the point (0, 0) where the x-axis and y-axis cross

look.title: Two Tables, One Test
look.text: Table A: x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 4, 8, 12. Table B: x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 5, 8, 11. In Table A, y ÷ x gives 4, 4, 4, so it is proportional and y = 4x. In Table B, y ÷ x gives 5, 4 and about 3.67, so it is not proportional. Table B is still linear: the slope is 3 and b = 2, so y = 3x + 2.
look.prompt: Make up a third table that is linear but not proportional, and a fourth that is proportional. Explain how the test y ÷ x tells them apart.

check.q: Which equation shows a proportional relationship?
check.why: A proportional relationship has the form y = kx with no added number, so its line passes through the origin. Only y = 4x fits.

check.q: A table shows x = 3, 5, 8 and y = 12, 20, 32. What is the constant of proportionality?
check.why: 12 ÷ 3 = 4, 20 ÷ 5 = 4 and 32 ÷ 8 = 4. Every y is 4 times its x, so k = 4.

check.q: Concert tickets cost $8 each plus a $5 order fee. Why is the total cost not proportional to the number of tickets?
choices: Because the slope is not constant
Because the cost for 0 tickets is $5, not $0
check.why: The equation is y = 8x + 5. At x = 0 the cost is 5, so the line misses the origin. A proportional line must pass through (0, 0).

lessons.title: Horizontal and Vertical Lines
lessons.mainIdea: A horizontal line has slope 0 and equation y = a number; a vertical line has an undefined slope and equation x = a number.
reading: A thermostat holds a room at 68°F for five hours. Graph the temperature against time: every point has y = 68, so the graph is a flat, *horizontal* line. Its equation is simply y = 68. Find its slope from (1, 68) and (4, 68): rise 68 − 68 = 0, run 4 − 1 = 3, slope 0/3 = 0. A horizontal line has slope 0 because the rise is always 0.

Now think of a wall standing straight up. Every point on it has the same x-value. A *vertical* line through (2, 1) and (2, 7) has the equation x = 2. Try the slope: rise 7 − 1 = 6, run 2 − 2 = 0, slope 6/0. You cannot divide by 0, so the slope is *undefined*. That is not the same as slope 0. A slope of 0 means flat, and an undefined slope means straight up and down.

Any line through (1, 5) and (4, 5) is horizontal, because the y-values match. Its equation is y = 5. Any line through (−3, 2) and (−3, 9) is vertical, because the x-values match. Its equation is x = −3. Look at which coordinate stays the same. If y stays the same, the line is horizontal. If x stays the same, the line is vertical.

The common mix-up is writing y = 2 for a vertical line at x = 2. Ask which axis the line is parallel to. A horizontal line runs parallel to the x-axis, but its equation names y, because y is the value that never changes. A vertical line runs parallel to the y-axis, and its equation names x. Also note that y = 68 fits y = mx + b with m = 0: y = 0x + 68. A vertical line does not fit that form at all, because there is no y in its equation.

words.d: flat, running left to right like the floor; a horizontal line has slope 0
straight up and down like a wall; a vertical line has an undefined slope
has no value; the slope of a vertical line is undefined because the run is 0 and you cannot divide by 0

look.title: Holding Steady
look.text: A thermostat holds a room at 68°F from 1 pm to 6 pm. On a graph with hours on the x-axis and degrees on the y-axis, the points (1, 68), (2, 68), (3, 68), (4, 68), (5, 68) and (6, 68) all sit at the same height. Between any two of them the rise is 0, so the slope is 0 and the equation is y = 68.
look.prompt: Now picture a graph of a wall's position: every point has x = 4 and y can be anything. Write the equation of that line and explain why its slope is undefined rather than 0.

check.q: A line passes through (2, 4) and (9, 4). Which describes it?
check.why: Both points have y = 4, so the line is horizontal with equation y = 4. Rise is 4 − 4 = 0, so the slope is 0.

check.q: What is the slope of the line x = 6?
check.why: Every point on x = 6 has the same x, so the run between any two points is 0. Dividing by 0 is not possible, so the slope is undefined.

check.q: Why is the slope of a horizontal line 0?
choices: Because the run between any two points is 0
Because the rise between any two points is 0
Because it never crosses the y-axis
Because it passes through the origin
check.why: All points on a horizontal line share one y-value, so rise = 0. Then slope = 0 ÷ run = 0.

review.q: What is the slope of the line through (0, 2) and (3, 11)?
What is the slope of the line y = −4x + 7?
review.why: In y = mx + b, the slope m is the coefficient of x, which is −4. The 7 is the y-intercept.

review.q: A road rises 5 feet for every 100 feet you move forward. What is its slope as a decimal?
review.why: Slope = rise ÷ run = 5 ÷ 100 = 0.05. The answer 20 comes from flipping the fraction.

review.q: A line passes through (0, 6) and (2, 0). What is its equation?
review.why: Slope = (0 − 6) ÷ (2 − 0) = −6/2 = −3. The y-intercept is 6. So y = −3x + 6.

review.q: Table A: x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 3, 6, 9. Table B: x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 4, 6, 8. Which is proportional?
choices: B, because y goes up by 2 each time
A, because y ÷ x is always 3
Both, because both are straight lines
review.why: In A, 3/1 = 6/2 = 9/3 = 3, so y = 3x. In B, 4/1 = 4 but 6/2 = 3, so B is linear but not proportional.

review.q: Are the points (1, 2), (3, 8) and (5, 12) on one straight line?
choices: No, because they do not start at 0
No, because the slopes 3 and 2 are different
review.why: From (1, 2) to (3, 8): 6/2 = 3. From (3, 8) to (5, 12): 4/2 = 2. Different slopes, so they are not on one line.

review.q: What is the equation of the vertical line through (−3, 5)?
review.why: On a vertical line, x never changes. Every point has x = −3, so the equation is x = −3.

review.q: To graph y = (1/2)x − 3, you plot (0, −3) first. Using the slope, which point comes next?
review.why: Slope 1/2 means right 2 and up 1. From (0, −3) that gives (2, −2). Check: (1/2) × 2 − 3 = 1 − 3 = −2.

chapters.title: Functions
chapters.bigQuestion: How can a rule, a table, an equation and a graph all tell the same story about how one amount depends on another?

story.title: The Graph of a Bike Ride
story.kicker: A coach draws one curve on the board, and the whole ride is in it: the hill, the flat road, even the water break.
paragraphs: Jordan rides with a youth cycling club on the trail along Lake Michigan. On Saturday the coach put a graph on the board with no labels except two: time in minutes along the bottom and distance from the start in miles up the side. One line ran across the graph. It began at zero, climbed slowly, then climbed faster, went perfectly flat for a while, and finally came back down to zero.

The coach asked the riders to tell the story of the ride from the picture alone. One rider said the slow climb at the start was the hill, because the group rode slowly there and the distance grew only a little each minute. Another said the steep part was the flat road by the water, where they went fast and covered miles quickly. Everyone agreed on the flat piece: that was the stop at the water fountain, when no one moved and the distance stayed the same.

Then the coach asked a harder question. The line came back down to zero at the end. Did the riders go backward? No, someone said. They turned around and rode home, so their distance from the start shrank until it was zero again. The graph did not show where they went. It showed how far from the start they were at each minute, and that was enough to tell the whole ride.

The coach wrote numbers on the graph. In the first 20 minutes, the group covered 3 miles up the hill. In the next 10 minutes, on the flat road, they covered 2.5 miles more. They stopped for 5 minutes. Then they rode all 5.5 miles home in 25 minutes. Jordan checked the speeds: 3 miles in 20 minutes is 9 miles per hour, and 2.5 miles in 10 minutes is 15 miles per hour. The steeper piece really was the faster piece.

A rule that gives one distance for each minute is called a function. The bike ride was a function drawn as a picture. This chapter shows what a function is, how to tell a function from a rule that is not one, and how to read a function whether it comes as words, a table, an equation or a graph.
story.think: Suppose the riders had stopped for water twice instead of once. How would the graph change? What would the graph look like if they rode home faster than they rode out?

lessons.title: One Output for Each Input
lessons.mainIdea: A function is a rule that gives exactly one output for each input.
reading: Press B4 on a vending machine and one item drops out, the same item every time. That machine is working like a *function*. A function is a rule that takes an *input* and gives back exactly one *output*. The input is what you put in, like the button. The output is what comes out, like the snack. If B4 sometimes gave chips and sometimes gave pretzels, the machine would not be a function.

Most functions in math are number rules. Take the rule output = 2 × input + 1. Put in 3: 2 × 3 + 1 = 7. Put in 10: 2 × 10 + 1 = 21. Put in 0: 2 × 0 + 1 = 1. Each input gives one and only one output. We usually call the input x and the output y, so this rule is y = 2x + 1. A table of inputs and outputs is one way to show it.

Try a rule with subtraction: output = 3 × input − 4. Input 1: 3 − 4 = −1. Input 2: 6 − 4 = 2. Input 5: 15 − 4 = 11. Input 10: 30 − 4 = 26. You can also run a function backward with one known output. If the output is 20, then 3 × input − 4 = 20, so 3 × input = 24 and the input is 8. Check: 3 × 8 − 4 = 24 − 4 = 20.

Functions do not have to use numbers. The rule that sends each student to their birthday is a function, because every student has exactly one birthday. The rule that sends each birthday to the students born on that day is not, because one date can belong to two students, and then the input has more than one output. The test is always the same: does each input have exactly one output?

words.d: a rule that gives exactly one output for each input
the number or thing you put into a rule; usually called x
the number or thing the rule gives back; usually called y

look.title: Running a Rule
look.text: The rule is: triple the input, then subtract 4. As an equation, y = 3x − 4. Input 1 gives 3 − 4 = −1. Input 2 gives 6 − 4 = 2. Input 5 gives 15 − 4 = 11. Input 10 gives 30 − 4 = 26. Every input gives one output, so the rule is a function.
look.prompt: Find the output for the input 7. Then find the input that gives the output 20, and check your answer by running it through the rule.

check.q: The rule is output = 4 × input − 3. What is the output for the input 5?
check.why: 4 × 5 − 3 = 20 − 3 = 17. Adding instead of subtracting gives 23.

check.q: Which rule is a function?
choices: Each student → every class the student takes
Each student → the student's height in inches
Each height → the students who are that tall
Each birthday → the students born that day
check.why: Every student has exactly one height, so each input has one output. The other rules can give several outputs for one input.

check.q: A function is a rule that gives ___.
choices: the same output for every input
exactly one output for each input
check.why: The definition of a function is one output for each input. The outputs can repeat, but an input cannot have two different outputs.

lessons.title: Function or Not?
lessons.mainIdea: A rule is not a function if any input has two different outputs; on a graph, a vertical line would hit the graph twice.
reading: A list of pairs shows inputs and outputs: (1, 3), (2, 5), (1, 7). Look for an input that *repeats*. The input 1 appears twice, once with output 3 and once with output 7. One input, two outputs: this is not a function. Now look at (1, 4), (2, 4), (3, 4). The output 4 repeats, but that is fine. Each input still has exactly one output, so this is a function.

That is the key difference. Repeated outputs are allowed. Repeated inputs with different outputs are not. A list like (2, 5), (3, 5), (4, 5) is a function even though the output never changes. A list like (2, 5), (2, 6) is not, because the input 2 cannot decide between 5 and 6.

On a graph, use the *vertical line test*. Imagine sliding a vertical line across the graph from left to right. Each vertical line marks one input, the x-value. If the line ever crosses the graph at two points, that input has two outputs, and the graph is not a function. A straight line that is not vertical always passes the test. A circle fails: a vertical line through its middle crosses it at the top and at the bottom.

Students sometimes run the test the wrong way, with a horizontal line. A horizontal line crossing twice only means two inputs share an output, which is allowed. Keep the line vertical. Students also sometimes think a table with a repeated output is not a function. Check the inputs, not the outputs.

words.d: a check on a graph: if any vertical line crosses the graph more than once, it is not a function
to appear again; an input that repeats with different outputs breaks the function rule

look.title: Three Lists
look.text: List A: (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6). List B: (1, 5), (2, 5), (3, 5). List C: (1, 2), (2, 4), (1, 6). In A every input has one output, so it is a function. In B the output 5 repeats, but each input still has one output, so it is a function too. In C the input 1 goes to both 2 and 6, so C is not a function.
look.prompt: Write your own list of four pairs that is not a function, and then change one number so that it becomes a function. Explain what you changed.

check.q: Is the list (2, 5), (3, 5), (4, 5) a function?
choices: Yes, because it is a straight line
Yes, because each input has exactly one output
check.why: The inputs 2, 3 and 4 are all different, and each has one output. Repeated outputs do not break the rule.

check.q: Is the list (1, 2), (2, 4), (1, 6) a function?
choices: No, because the input 1 has two outputs
Yes, because each pair is different
No, because the output 4 appears only once
check.why: The input 1 goes to 2 and also to 6. One input with two outputs means it is not a function.

check.q: A vertical line crosses a graph at two points. What does that tell you?
choices: The graph is a straight line
The graph is not a function
check.why: A vertical line marks one input. Two crossings mean that input has two outputs, so the graph fails the vertical line test.

lessons.title: Four Ways to Show a Rule
lessons.mainIdea: The same function can be given in words, as a table of values, as an equation or as a graph, and you can move between them.
reading: A pool starts with 500 gallons and loses 3 gallons every hour through a leak. That sentence is the function in words. Turn it into an *equation*: let x be the hours and y the gallons. Each hour takes away 3, so y = 500 − 3x. Now make a *table of values*. At x = 0, y = 500. At x = 1, y = 497. At x = 2, y = 494. At x = 10, y = 500 − 30 = 470.

Plot those table rows as points, (0, 500), (1, 497), (2, 494), (10, 470), and connect them: that is the graph. It is a straight line that starts at 500 on the y-axis and falls 3 for every hour. Words, equation, table and graph are four views of one function. Each view is good for something. The equation gives any value fast. The table shows a few exact values. The graph shows the shape at a glance.

You can go in any direction. From a table with x = 0, 1, 2 and y = 9, 7, 5, find the rule. The y-value at x = 0 is 9, so the starting amount is 9. Each step down is 2, so the rule is y = 9 − 2x, which is the same as y = −2x + 9. From words like start with 12 and add 5 each week, write y = 5x + 12, where x counts the weeks.

A common slip is reading the first row of a table as the starting amount when that row is not x = 0. If a table begins at x = 1, the starting amount is one step earlier. Another slip is mixing the two numbers in the words: start with 12 and add 5 each week is y = 5x + 12, not y = 12x + 5. The number that repeats every week is the one that multiplies x.

words.d: a math sentence with an equal sign, like y = 500 − 3x, that gives the rule of a function
a list of inputs with their matching outputs, usually in two columns

look.title: The Leaking Pool
look.cite: Table of values from y = 500 − 3x, a pool losing 3 gallons an hour, made for this lesson
look.prompt: How many gallons are left after 20 hours? Use the equation, then check by continuing the pattern in the table. Describe what the graph looks like.

check.q: Start with 12, then add 5 each week. Which equation is this?
check.why: The 5 is added every week, so it multiplies the number of weeks x. The 12 is the starting amount. So y = 5x + 12.

check.q: A table shows x = 0, 1, 2 and y = 9, 7, 5. What is the equation?
check.why: At x = 0, y = 9, so the starting value is 9. Each step, y drops by 2, so the rate is −2. So y = −2x + 9.

check.q: Using y = 500 − 3x, how many gallons are in the pool after 15 hours?
check.why: 3 × 15 = 45, and 500 − 45 = 455. Adding instead of subtracting gives 545.

lessons.title: Linear Functions
lessons.mainIdea: A linear function changes by the same amount for each step in x, so its graph is a straight line and its equation is y = mx + b.
reading: A table shows x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and y = 4, 7, 10, 13. Look at how y changes as x goes up by 1: 7 − 4 = 3, 10 − 7 = 3, 13 − 10 = 3. The change is always 3. A function that changes by the same amount for each equal step in x has a *constant rate*, and it is a *linear function*. Its graph is a straight line, and its equation can be written as y = mx + b.

For this table, m is the constant rate, 3, and b is the value at x = 0, which is 4. So y = 3x + 4. Check: at x = 3, 3 × 3 + 4 = 9 + 4 = 13. It matches. At x = 10, the equation gives 3 × 10 + 4 = 34, which the table would reach if it kept going.

You can spot a linear function in any form. In words: a fixed amount added or taken away every unit of time, like 3 gallons every hour. In a table: equal steps in x give equal steps in y. In an equation: x appears only multiplied by a number and maybe added to a number, like y = 6x − 1 or y = 500 − 3x. In a graph: a straight line.

The classic mistake is deciding a function is linear because y keeps going up. Going up is not enough. It must go up by the same amount every step. The table x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and y = 1, 2, 4, 8 goes up every time, but the steps are 1, 2 and 4. That is not a constant rate, so it is not linear. Always compute the differences before you decide.

words.d: a function whose graph is a straight line; it has a constant rate of change and can be written y = mx + b
a rate that stays the same: y changes by the same amount for each equal step in x

look.title: Spot the Line
look.text: Table A: x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and y = 2, 5, 8, 11. Table B: x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and y = 1, 2, 4, 8. In Table A, y rises by 3 each step: 5 − 2, 8 − 5 and 11 − 8 are all 3, so A is linear with equation y = 3x + 2. In Table B, the steps are 1, 2 and 4. They keep changing, so B is not linear.
look.prompt: Extend both tables to x = 4 and x = 5. Which table's next values can you predict with y = mx + b? What rule fits Table B instead?

check.q: A table shows x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and y = 1, 4, 7, 10. Is the function linear?
choices: No, because y is not a multiple of x
Yes, because y rises by 3 each step
No, because it does not start at 0
Yes, because y rises by 1 each step
check.why: 4 − 1 = 3, 7 − 4 = 3 and 10 − 7 = 3. A constant change of 3 means linear, with y = 3x + 1.

check.q: For the linear function y = 3x + 4, what is y when x = 10?
check.why: 3 × 10 = 30, and 30 + 4 = 34. The answer 70 comes from adding 3 and 4 first and then multiplying by 10.

check.q: Which equation gives a linear function?
check.why: In y = 6x − 1, x is only multiplied by 6 and then 1 is subtracted, which is the form y = mx + b. The others have x squared, x as an exponent or x in a denominator.

lessons.title: Nonlinear Functions
lessons.mainIdea: A nonlinear function does not change by the same amount each step, so its graph is a curve, not a straight line.
reading: The area of a *square* with side x is y = x^2, which means x times x. Make a table: x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 gives y = 0, 1, 4, 9, 16. Now find the changes: 1 − 0 = 1, 4 − 1 = 3, 9 − 4 = 5, 16 − 9 = 7. The steps are 1, 3, 5, 7, growing each time. The rate is not constant, so this is a *nonlinear* function. Plot the points and you get a *curve* that bends upward, not a straight line.

Doubling is another nonlinear pattern. A rule where each output is twice the one before gives x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = 2, 4, 8, 16. The changes are 2, 4 and 8. Again the steps grow. The equation is y = 2^x, 2 to the power x. It grows faster and faster, which is why doubling patterns get huge so quickly.

Nonlinear functions are still functions. Each input has exactly one output: the square of 6 is 36 and only 36. What makes them different from linear functions is only the rate. A linear function adds the same amount each step. A nonlinear function does not. In a graph, that shows up as bending. In an equation, it shows up as x being squared, used as an exponent, or placed under a fraction bar.

A common mistake is calling y = x^2 linear because its table goes up steadily and its equation looks simple. Compute the differences and the bending shows: 1, 3, 5, 7. Another mistake is using the linear method on a nonlinear table. If someone takes the first step of y = x^2, which is 1, and predicts y = 1x, they will get 6 for x = 6 instead of 36.

words.d: not linear; a function whose rate of change is not constant and whose graph is not a straight line
a graph that bends instead of running straight
a number times itself; the square of 5 is 5 × 5 = 25, written 5^2

look.title: Side Length and Area
look.cite: Area of a square = side × side, computed for sides 1 to 5 cm
look.prompt: Find the change in area from each row to the next. Are the changes constant? What does that tell you about the graph of area against side length?

check.q: For y = x^2, what is y when x = 6?
check.why: x^2 means x × x, so 6 × 6 = 36. The answer 12 comes from doubling instead of squaring.

check.q: A table shows x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = 2, 4, 8, 16. Which describes it?
choices: Linear, because y doubles each time
Nonlinear, because the changes 2, 4, 8 are not constant
Nonlinear, because 16 is a big number
check.why: The changes are 4 − 2 = 2, 8 − 4 = 4, 16 − 8 = 8. Since the change keeps growing, the function is nonlinear.

check.q: The graph of a linear function is a ___, and the graph of y = x^2 is a ___.
check.why: A constant rate draws a straight line. The changing rate of y = x^2 makes its graph bend into a curve.

lessons.title: Rate of Change and Initial Value
lessons.mainIdea: Every linear function has a rate of change, which is its slope, and an initial value, which is its output when the input is 0.
reading: A candle is 20 cm tall and burns down 2 cm every hour. Two numbers describe this function. The *initial value* is the height at the start, when 0 hours have passed: 20 cm. The *rate of change* is −2 cm per hour, negative because the height goes down. The equation is y = 20 − 2x, or y = −2x + 20. After 4 hours: 20 − 8 = 12 cm. The candle is gone when y = 0, which is 20 ÷ 2 = 10 hours.

From an equation, read the two numbers straight off. In y = 12x + 30, the rate of change is 12 and the initial value is 30. That could be a gym that costs $30 to join and $12 a month. From a graph, the initial value is where the line crosses the y-axis, and the rate is the slope.

From a table without x = 0, do a little work. Say x = 2 gives y = 19 and x = 5 gives y = 31. Rate = (31 − 19) ÷ (5 − 2) = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 per unit. To find the initial value, go back from x = 2 to x = 0, which is 2 steps of 4, or 8: 19 − 8 = 11. So the initial value is 11 and the equation is y = 4x + 11. Check: 4 × 5 + 11 = 31.

Keep the two numbers separate in your head. The rate answers how fast it changes. The initial value answers where it starts. A common slip is reporting the first number in the table as the initial value, like 19 above, when x is not 0 in that row. Another is dropping the negative sign on a decreasing rate: the candle's rate is −2, and writing +2 would make it grow.

words.d: the output when the input is 0; the starting amount, which is b in y = mx + b
how much the output changes for each 1 unit of input; the slope m in y = mx + b

look.title: The Burning Candle
look.text: A candle is 20 cm tall and burns down 2 cm each hour. The initial value is 20 cm, the height at 0 hours. The rate of change is −2 cm per hour. The equation is y = 20 − 2x. After 4 hours the candle is 20 − 8 = 12 cm. It is completely gone when 20 − 2x = 0, which happens at x = 10 hours.
look.prompt: A second candle is 15 cm tall and burns 3 cm an hour. Write its equation, name its rate and initial value, and find when it is gone. Which candle lasts longer?

check.q: In y = 12x + 30, what is the initial value?
check.why: The initial value is y when x = 0: 12 × 0 + 30 = 30. The 12 is the rate of change.

check.q: A table shows x = 2, y = 19 and x = 5, y = 31. What are the rate of change and the initial value?
check.why: Rate = (31 − 19) ÷ (5 − 2) = 4. Going back 2 steps from x = 2: 19 − 2 × 4 = 11. So the initial value is 11.

check.q: A candle 20 cm tall burns 2 cm each hour. What is the rate of change of its height?
check.why: The height drops 2 cm for every 1 hour, so the rate is −2 cm per hour. The 20 is the initial value.

lessons.title: Comparing Two Functions
lessons.mainIdea: To compare functions given in different ways, find each one's rate of change and initial value, then compare those numbers.
reading: Two text plans are on offer. Plan A comes as an equation: y = 0.10x + 20, where x is the number of texts and y the monthly cost in dollars. Plan B comes as a table: 0 texts cost $15, 100 texts cost $27, 200 texts cost $39. To make a fair *comparison*, get both plans into the same terms: a rate and an initial value.

Plan A's rate is 0.10 dollars per text and its initial value is $20. For Plan B, the rate is (27 − 15) ÷ (100 − 0) = 12 ÷ 100 = 0.12 dollars per text, and the initial value is $15, since the table shows x = 0. So B starts cheaper but grows faster. Its graph is *steeper*. At 100 texts, A costs 10 + 20 = 30 and B costs 27, so B is cheaper. At 300 texts, A costs 30 + 20 = 50 and B costs 15 + 36 = 51, so A is cheaper.

The same idea works for any pair. Function A: y = 5x + 2. Function B is a table: x = 0, 1, 2 and y = 10, 13, 16. B's rate is 3 and its initial value is 10. A's rate is 5 and its initial value is 2. A grows faster because 5 is greater than 3, even though B starts higher. At x = 4, A gives 5 × 4 + 2 = 22 and B gives 10 + 3 × 4 = 22. That is the point where they meet.

Do not compare the wrong numbers. B starts at 10 and A starts at 2, but that says nothing about which grows faster. Growth is the rate. Also, do not read a rate from a table without dividing by the change in x. Plan B's cost rose 12 dollars, but over 100 texts, so the rate is 0.12 per text, not 12.

words.d: looking at two things side by side to see how they are alike and different
having a bigger slope; a steeper line changes faster

look.title: Plan B by the Numbers
look.cite: Example plan made for this lesson: $15 a month plus $0.12 per text
look.prompt: Plan A is y = 0.10x + 20. Find Plan A's cost at 500 texts and compare it with the table. Which plan is cheaper at 500 texts, and by how much?

check.q: Plan B costs $15 for 0 texts and $27 for 100 texts. What is its rate of change in dollars per text?
check.why: (27 − 15) ÷ (100 − 0) = 12 ÷ 100 = 0.12 dollars per text. The answer 12 forgets to divide by the 100 texts.

check.q: Function A is y = 5x + 2. Function B is the table x = 0, 1, 2 and y = 10, 13, 16. Which grows faster?
choices: They grow at the same rate
A, because its rate 5 is greater than B's rate 3
check.why: B's rate is 13 − 10 = 3 per step. A's rate is 5. Growth is about the rate, not the starting value.

check.q: At x = 4, Function A gives 22 and Function B gives 22. What does that mean?
choices: Both functions have the same output at x = 4
A is always larger than B
B is always larger than A
check.why: Equal outputs at one input mean the graphs cross there. With different rates, the functions differ everywhere else.

lessons.title: Sketching a Graph From a Story
lessons.mainIdea: Each part of a story becomes a segment of the graph: rising, falling or flat, steep or gentle.
reading: Ana walks to the store, shops, and jogs home. Graph her distance from home against time. She walks 0.5 mile in 10 minutes: the first *segment* rises from (0, 0) to (10, 0.5). She shops for 15 minutes: the distance stays at 0.5, so the segment is flat from (10, 0.5) to (25, 0.5). She jogs home in 5 minutes: the last segment falls from (25, 0.5) to (30, 0).

The slopes tell the speeds. Walking: 0.5 mile ÷ 10 minutes = 0.05 mile per minute. Jogging home: 0.5 ÷ 5 = 0.1 mile per minute, twice as fast. So the jog-home segment is twice as *steep* as the walk-there segment, and it goes down because Ana is getting closer to home. The flat segment has slope 0: no motion.

A bathtub works the same way. Fill it for 8 minutes: the water level rises. Sit in it for 20 minutes: the level stays put, a flat segment. Pull the plug and it drains in 4 minutes: the level falls, and since 4 minutes is shorter than 8, the draining segment is steeper than the filling one. Three parts of the story, three segments: rise, flat, fall.

When sketching, ask three questions for each part of the story. Is the amount going up, going down or staying the same? Is it changing fast or slowly? How long does that part last? Going up means the segment rises, fast means steep, and the time sets how wide the segment is. A common mistake is drawing the return trip going up again. In a distance-from-home graph, coming home means the distance shrinks, so the segment falls.

words.d: one straight piece of a graph, between two points where the story changes
rising or falling quickly; a steep segment has a large slope

look.title: The Bathtub Graph
look.text: A tub fills for 8 minutes, then someone soaks for 20 minutes, then the tub drains in 4 minutes. On a graph of water level against time, the first segment rises from 0 to 8 minutes. The second is flat from 8 to 28 minutes. The third falls from 28 to 32 minutes. Filling took 8 minutes and draining took 4, so the falling segment is steeper than the rising one.
look.prompt: Sketch the bathtub graph on paper. Then sketch a second graph where the tub drains slowly over 16 minutes instead of 4. What changes, and what stays the same?

check.q: On a graph of distance from home against time, what does a flat segment mean?
check.why: A flat segment has slope 0, so the distance from home is not changing. The person is stopped.

check.q: Ana walks 0.5 mile to the store in 10 minutes and jogs the same 0.5 mile home in 5 minutes. Which segment is steeper?
check.why: Walking: 0.5 ÷ 10 = 0.05 mile per minute. Jogging: 0.5 ÷ 5 = 0.1 mile per minute. The faster trip makes the steeper segment.

check.q: A tub fills, then sits full, then drains. What is the shape of its water-level graph?
check.why: Filling raises the level, sitting keeps it the same, and draining lowers it: rise, flat, fall.

lessons.title: Telling a Story From a Graph
lessons.mainIdea: Read a graph segment by segment: steeper means faster, flat means a pause, and falling means the amount is decreasing.
reading: Return to the bike ride graph. From 0 to 20 minutes the distance rises from 0 to 3 miles. From 20 to 30 minutes it rises from 3 to 5.5 miles. From 30 to 35 minutes it stays at 5.5. From 35 to 60 minutes it falls from 5.5 back to 0. Four segments, four parts of the story: a slow climb, a fast stretch, a *pause*, and the ride home.

Turn each segment into a speed. First: 3 miles in 20 minutes. There are 3 twenty-minute pieces in an hour, so that is 3 × 3 = 9 miles per hour. Second: 2.5 miles in 10 minutes, and there are 6 ten-minute pieces in an hour, so 2.5 × 6 = 15 miles per hour. Third: 0 miles in 5 minutes, speed 0. Fourth: 5.5 miles in 25 minutes. Divide 5.5 by 25 to get 0.22 mile per minute, and 0.22 × 60 = 13.2 miles per hour.

Now compare. The steepest rising segment is the second, at 15 miles per hour, so that was the fastest part of the ride out. The flat segment is the water stop. The last segment is *decreasing*, which means the riders were getting closer to the start. It was fairly steep too, 13.2 miles per hour, so they rode home almost as fast as their fastest stretch.

Two habits keep the story honest. First, read the axes before anything else. If the y-axis were speed instead of distance, a flat segment would mean steady speed, not a stop. Second, compare slopes, not heights. A segment that ends at a high number is not automatically the fast one. The 25-minute ride home covered the most miles, but the 10-minute stretch was faster.

words.d: a stop; on a distance graph, a flat segment where the distance does not change
going down; a decreasing segment falls as you move right on the graph

look.title: The Balloon's Height
look.text: A graph shows a toy balloon's height above the ground against time. For the first 4 minutes the line rises steadily to 60 feet. For the next 3 minutes it stays level at 60 feet. Then in 1 minute it drops all the way to 0. The rising segment is gentle, the flat segment shows the balloon hovering, and the last segment is very steep because 60 feet of change happened in only 1 minute.
look.prompt: Tell the story of the balloon in three sentences, one for each segment. Then find the rate of the first segment in feet per minute and the rate of the last segment.

check.q: On the bike ride graph, the distance goes from 3 miles to 5.5 miles between minute 20 and minute 30. What was the speed?
check.why: 2.5 miles in 10 minutes. There are 6 ten-minute pieces in an hour, so 2.5 × 6 = 15 miles per hour.

check.q: The distance stays at 5.5 miles from minute 30 to minute 35. What happened?
check.why: A flat segment means the distance is not changing, so the riders were not moving. That is the water stop.

check.q: Which segment of the bike ride was the fastest?
check.why: The speeds are 9, 15, 0 and 13.2 miles per hour. The greatest is 15 mph, from minute 20 to minute 30.

lessons.title: Describing a Function in Words
lessons.mainIdea: You can describe any function by saying where it is increasing or decreasing, and whether it is linear or nonlinear.
reading: Sometimes you do not need numbers, just the shape. Throw a ball straight up. Its height is *increasing* while it rises, then *decreasing* while it falls. The graph of height against time is a curve, so the function is nonlinear. The whole description is: nonlinear, increasing at first, then decreasing. Those few words tell most of what happens.

A savings account starts with $50 and gets $10 every week. The amount is always going up, and it goes up by the same $10 each week. So the function is linear and increasing. The graph is a straight line rising to the right. A phone battery that loses 1% every 4 minutes during a video is linear and decreasing: a straight line falling to the right.

The temperature on a summer day in Chicago might be 65°F at 6 am, rise to 84°F by 3 pm, and fall to 70°F by midnight. The function is increasing on the *interval* from 6 am to 3 pm and decreasing after 3 pm. It is nonlinear, because the temperature does not rise by the same amount every hour. It climbs quickly at midmorning and slowly near the peak.

Two things to watch. First, increasing and decreasing describe parts of a graph, so name the interval: increasing from 6 am to 3 pm, not just increasing. Second, linear and nonlinear describe the whole shape. A function can be nonlinear and still increasing everywhere, like y = 2^x. A function can be linear and decreasing, like the battery. Mix the words as the graph requires.

words.d: going up; the output gets larger as the input gets larger
going down; the output gets smaller as the input gets larger
a stretch of input values, like from 6 am to 3 pm

look.title: A Day of Temperatures
look.text: Picture a graph of temperature against time for one summer day. It starts at 65°F at 6 am, climbs to a high of 84°F at 3 pm, and drops to 70°F by midnight. The rise is a curve that gets flatter near the top, and the fall is a curve too. The function is increasing from 6 am to 3 pm, decreasing from 3 pm to midnight, and nonlinear throughout.
look.prompt: Describe the graph of a ball thrown into the air the same way: name the intervals where the height is increasing and decreasing, and say whether it is linear or nonlinear.

check.q: A ball's height goes up and then comes down, following a curve. Which words describe the function?
check.why: A curve means nonlinear. The height rises and then falls, so it is increasing, then decreasing.

check.q: A savings account starts at $50 and gains $10 every week. Which words describe it?
check.why: The same $10 is added each week, which is a constant rate, so it is linear. The amount grows, so it is increasing.

check.q: The temperature rises from 6 am to 3 pm and falls after that. On which interval is the function decreasing?
check.why: Decreasing means the output goes down. The temperature goes down only after the 3 pm peak.

review.q: The rule is output = 3 × input + 2. What is the output for the input 6?
Which list of pairs is NOT a function?
review.why: In the last list the input 4 has two outputs, 1 and 3. Repeated outputs, as in the first list, are allowed.

review.q: A table shows x = 0, 1, 2 and y = 5, 9, 13. Is the function linear, and what is its equation?
choices: No, because y is not a multiple of x
No, because it is a curve
review.why: y rises by 4 each step, a constant rate, so it is linear. The value at x = 0 is 5. So y = 4x + 5.

review.q: For y = x^2, how much does y change when x goes from 3 to 4?
review.why: 3^2 = 9 and 4^2 = 16. The change is 16 − 9 = 7.

review.q: What is the initial value of the function y = 8x + 25?
review.why: The initial value is y when x = 0, which is 8 × 0 + 25 = 25.

review.q: Function A is y = 2x + 9. Function B is the table x = 0, 1, 2 and y = 1, 5, 9. Which has the greater rate of change?
review.why: B's rate is 5 − 1 = 4 per step. A's rate is 2. So B changes faster, even though A starts higher.

review.q: On a graph of distance from home against time, a segment that falls means the person is ___.
review.why: Falling means the distance from home is decreasing, so the person is getting closer to home.

review.q: A linear function has x = 3, y = 14 and x = 7, y = 26. What is its rate of change?

chapters.title: Systems of Equations
chapters.bigQuestion: When two rules are both true at once, how do you find the one pair of numbers that satisfies them both?

story.title: When Does the Tortoise Get Caught?
story.kicker: An old fable becomes a math problem the moment you draw both runners on the same graph.
paragraphs: Everyone knows the fable: the tortoise and the hare agree to race, the hare is far faster, and the hare loses anyway by stopping for a nap. Ms. Okafor's class in Chicago decided to make the story into numbers. They gave the tortoise a head start of 300 meters and a steady speed of 1 meter per second. They gave the hare a speed of 5 meters per second, starting from the line. The question was simple. If the hare never naps, when does it catch the tortoise?

The class drew a graph with seconds along the bottom and meters from the starting line up the side. The tortoise's line began at 300 and climbed gently, 1 meter for each second. The hare's line began at 0 and climbed steeply, 5 meters for each second. Two lines, two rules. Each line by itself told where one runner was at any moment. The interesting spot was where the lines crossed.

At the crossing, both runners are the same distance from the line at the same time. That is the catch. The students read the point off the graph: about 75 seconds, about 375 meters. Then they checked with the equations. Tortoise: 300 + 1 × 75 = 375. Hare: 5 × 75 = 375. Both rules gave the same number, so the crossing was exact. The hare catches the tortoise 75 seconds into the race, 375 meters down the track.

Then someone added the nap. Suppose the hare stops at 60 seconds and sleeps for 100 seconds. The hare's line goes flat at 300 meters from second 60 to second 160, while the tortoise's line keeps climbing. At second 160 the tortoise is at 300 + 160 = 460 meters, far ahead. Now there is a new crossing to find, and a new question: does the hare still catch up before the finish?

A pair of rules that must both be true at once is called a system of equations. Its solution is the point where the graphs meet. This chapter shows how to find that point by graphing, by substitution and by elimination, how to tell when there is no such point or many of them, and how to use systems for phone plans, tickets and coins.
story.think: Without the nap, the hare catches the tortoise at 75 seconds. If the tortoise's head start were doubled to 600 meters, would the catch happen at double the time? Work it out and explain.

lessons.title: What a System Is
lessons.mainIdea: A system of equations is two equations that must both be true, and its solution is the one pair (x, y) that works in both.
reading: Two numbers add up to 10, and their difference is 4. Call the larger number x and the smaller y. The first sentence says x + y = 10. The second says x − y = 4. Together the two equations form a *system of equations*. Many pairs fit the first equation alone: (5, 5), (8, 2), (9, 1). Many fit the second alone: (6, 2), (8, 4), (10, 6). The *solution of a system* is a pair that fits both at the same time.

Test (8, 2). First equation: 8 + 2 = 10, true. Second: 8 − 2 = 6, not 4. So (8, 2) is not a solution. Test (7, 3). First: 7 + 3 = 10, true. Second: 7 − 3 = 4, true. Both equations are satisfied, so (7, 3) is the solution. The two numbers are 7 and 3.

On a graph, each equation is a line, and every point on that line makes its equation true. The solution of the system is the point where the two lines cross, because that is the only point on both lines. For x + y = 10 and x − y = 4, the lines cross at (7, 3). There is no other point on both lines, so there is no other solution.

To check a proposed solution, substitute it into both equations, not just one. Take y = x − 4 and y = 2x − 9 with the point (5, 1). First: 5 − 4 = 1, true. Second: 2 × 5 − 9 = 10 − 9 = 1, true. So (5, 1) is a solution. A point that passes one equation and fails the other is not a solution. Both checks must pass.

words.d: two or more equations that must all be true at the same time
a pair of values (x, y) that makes every equation in the system true

look.title: Sum 15, Difference 3
look.text: Two numbers have a sum of 15 and a difference of 3. With x the larger and y the smaller: x + y = 15 and x − y = 3. Try (9, 6). Sum: 9 + 6 = 15, true. Difference: 9 − 6 = 3, true. So (9, 6) is the solution. Try (10, 5): the sum is 15, but the difference is 5, so it fails the second equation.
look.prompt: Two numbers have a sum of 20 and a difference of 8. Write the two equations, find the pair that works in both, and show both checks.

check.q: Is (7, 3) a solution of the system x + y = 10 and x − y = 4?
choices: It fits only the first equation
check.why: Substitute into both: 7 + 3 = 10 is true and 7 − 3 = 4 is true. Both pass, so (7, 3) is the solution.

check.q: What is the solution of a system of two equations?
choices: a pair (x, y) that makes both equations true
the y-intercept of the first line
the slope of the second line
check.why: A solution must satisfy every equation in the system. On a graph, that is the point where the lines cross.

check.q: Is (5, 1) a solution of y = x − 4 and y = 2x − 9?
choices: No, it fails the second equation
No, it fails the first equation
There is no way to tell
check.why: First: 5 − 4 = 1. Second: 2 × 5 − 9 = 1. Both equal the y-value 1, so (5, 1) satisfies both.

lessons.title: Solving by Graphing
lessons.mainIdea: Graph both lines on one grid; the point where they cross is the solution, and substituting checks it.
reading: Solve the system y = 2x + 1 and y = −x + 7 by graphing. Graph the first line: start at (0, 1) and use slope 2 to reach (1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 7). Graph the second: start at (0, 7) and use slope −1 to reach (1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4). The point (2, 5) is on both lists. That is the *intersection*, where the two lines cross, so the solution is (2, 5).

Always check the *point of intersection* in both equations. First: 2 × 2 + 1 = 5. Second: −2 + 7 = 5. Both give 5, so (2, 5) is exact. If a check fails, either the graph was drawn wrong or the crossing was read wrong. Redraw with care and look again.

Try y = x + 3 and y = 3x − 1. First line: (0, 3), (1, 4), (2, 5), (3, 6). Second line: (0, −1), (1, 2), (2, 5), (3, 8). They share (2, 5). Check: 2 + 3 = 5 and 3 × 2 − 1 = 5. Notice that the second line starts lower but climbs faster, so it catches the first, just like the hare catching the tortoise.

Graphing is quick and it shows the picture, but it has limits. It works best when the crossing lands on a *lattice point* with whole-number coordinates. If the lines cross at something like (1.4, 5.2), reading it off a grid gives only an estimate. The next lesson deals with that. Also watch for careless slopes: one line drawn with the wrong slope will cross in the wrong place, and the check will catch it.

words.d: the place where two lines cross
the (x, y) coordinates of the crossing point; the solution of the system
a point on a grid whose coordinates are both whole numbers

look.title: Two Lines, One Crossing
look.text: Graph y = x + 3 and y = 3x − 1 on the same grid. The first passes through (0, 3), (1, 4), (2, 5) and (3, 6). The second passes through (0, −1), (1, 2), (2, 5) and (3, 8). Both lists contain (2, 5), so the lines cross there. Check: 2 + 3 = 5 and 3 × 2 − 1 = 5.
look.prompt: Graph y = 2x and y = −x + 6 on grid paper. Where do they cross? Substitute the crossing point into both equations to prove it.

check.q: Where do the lines y = 2x + 1 and y = −x + 7 cross?
check.why: At x = 2, the first gives 2 × 2 + 1 = 5 and the second gives −2 + 7 = 5. Both lines pass through (2, 5).

check.q: Where do the lines y = x + 3 and y = 3x − 1 cross?
check.why: At x = 2, y = 2 + 3 = 5 and y = 3 × 2 − 1 = 5. The point (1, 4) is on the first line only, since 3 × 1 − 1 = 2.

check.q: Solving by graphing works best when ___.
choices: the crossing point has whole-number coordinates
check.why: A crossing at a lattice point can be read exactly from the grid. Fraction coordinates can only be estimated from a graph.

lessons.title: Estimating and Checking
lessons.mainIdea: When the crossing is not on a grid corner, estimate it from the graph, then use algebra to find the exact point and check it.
reading: Graph y = 3x + 1 and y = −2x + 8. The first line rises steeply from (0, 1). The second falls from (0, 8). They cross somewhere between x = 1 and x = 2, a little above y = 5. From the picture, a reasonable *estimate* is (1.5, 5). But is that exact? *Check by substitution*: 3 × 1.5 + 1 = 5.5, and −2 × 1.5 + 8 = 5. The two equations give different values, so (1.5, 5) is close but not the true crossing.

To get the exact point, set the two expressions for y equal, since y is the same at the crossing: 3x + 1 = −2x + 8. Add 2x to both sides: 5x + 1 = 8. Subtract 1: 5x = 7. Divide: x = 7/5 = 1.4. Then y = 3 × 1.4 + 1 = 4.2 + 1 = 5.2. Check in the second equation: −2 × 1.4 + 8 = −2.8 + 8 = 5.2. Both agree, so the exact solution is (1.4, 5.2).

The estimate was not wasted. It told us the answer should be near x = 1.5 and y = 5, so the algebra result of (1.4, 5.2) makes sense. If the algebra had given (14, 52), the graph would show that something went wrong. Use the graph to predict the size of the answer, and use algebra to nail it down.

Two mistakes are common here. One is trusting a graph reading as exact just because it looks right. Always substitute into both equations. The other is checking only one equation. The point (2, 5) fits y = 2x + 1 perfectly, but for y = −x + 6 it gives −2 + 6 = 4, not 5. A point must pass both checks to be a solution.

words.d: a careful guess that is close to the exact value, like reading a point from a graph
put the x and y values into each equation and see whether both sides come out equal

look.title: Close, but Is It Exact?
look.text: Graph y = 2x + 1 and y = −x + 6. The first rises from (0, 1) through (1, 3) and (2, 5). The second falls from (0, 6) through (1, 5) and (2, 4). The lines cross between x = 1 and x = 2, near y = 4.5. The point (2, 5) is a tempting guess, but in the second equation −2 + 6 = 4, not 5. Setting 2x + 1 = −x + 6 gives 3x = 5, so x = 5/3, about 1.67, and y is about 4.33.
